implementation_notes: The BCL supplies the whole structure: a readonly Lazy<T> field constructed with a factory computes once under ExecutionAndPublication (the default mode) and returns the same value to all threads; LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly lets racing threads compute and publishes the first winner, and None disables thread safety entirely. The classic null-marker plus lock structure is replaced by the type; it is still justified only in pre-.NET-4 code or when even one Lazy<T> allocation per instance is too much. Exception behaviour is part of the mode: with a factory, a thrown exception is cached and rethrown on every later Value access.
pitfalls: Exceptions from the factory are cached and rethrown on every subsequent Value access (the same exception instance, so its original stack trace no longer points at the retry) - if the failure may be transient, do not wrap a flaky factory in Lazy<T>.

Recursive access to Value from inside the initialisation method throws InvalidOperationException instead of blocking, so an initialiser that reaches the same property (directly or through a callback) fails at runtime rather than deadlocking.
LazyThreadSafetyMode.None is a real footgun in server code: it silently removes all publication guarantees, and PublicationOnly can run the factory several times, discarding the losers.
IsValueCreated is for diagnostics only; using it as an access guard reintroduces the race Lazy<T> was chosen to remove.

variants.name: LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized (allocation-free)
variants.implementation_notes: For struct fields, arrays of cells, or hot types where a Lazy<T> object per field is unacceptable, LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized(ref target, factory) gives the same once-only semantics without allocating a wrapper; the field itself is the cell and the initialisation uses the runtime's thread-safe publication step. This replaces the Lazy<T> wrapper, not the pattern - it is still a real once-primitive, not a hand-written flag test.
pitfalls: EnsureInitialized operates on the field by reference: on a struct property (a copy) it initialises the copy and the value is lost - pass the actual field, not a property or a copied value.

It offers no thread-safety mode and no exception-caching policy parameter: do not assume Lazy<T> semantics (mode selection, cached factory exceptions) when switching an existing field to EnsureInitialized.

Because it is a per-field API there is no shared accessor abstraction: initialising the same value from two call sites recreates the double-build the pattern removes, and each cell needs its own review.

variants.name: Hand-written double-checked locking on a volatile field
variants.idiom_name: volatile field plus lock in the slow path
variants.implementation_notes: Before .NET 4 and in the rare hot path where an extra wrapper allocation hurts, the classic form is still written by hand: a volatile field tested outside the lock, the initialisation inside the lock and a second test inside it. The volatile (or Volatile.Read/Interlocked) part is what makes the unsynchronised fast path legal in the .NET memory model; without it the pattern publishes partially constructed objects. Prefer Lazy<T>/LazyInitializer in all new code.
pitfalls: Dropping volatile (or the equivalent barrier) makes the fast path a cache-coherency bug that appears only on weak memory models - the single most common defect of this variant.
The lock is per-gate: a second lock protects nothing, and lock(this)/lock(typeof(T)) invite external contention or deadlock.
The field must be re-read before returning, otherwise the local read outside the lock can hand back null after another thread initialised it.
